opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is just that we're not very loud about it. There's a cultural thing at DeepMind, and it's partly inherited from Google more broadly, where the default is to do the work and publish the paper, and then maybe there's a blog post, and that's kind of it. We don't tend to do a lot of the public-facing narrative-building that some other labs do. That's not necessarily a deliberate choice to stay quiet. It's more that nobody's job is really to go out and tell the story, and researchers would generally rather be doing research.

A second factor is that a lot of what we do is fairly unglamorous. Take something like our work on dangerous capability evaluations, or the Frontier Safety Framework, or a lot of the amplified oversight and debate work. It's important, and I think it matters a lot for how things actually go, but it doesn't produce a single flashy result that goes viral. A lot of it is incremental: figuring out how to make an evaluation actually reliable, or working out the details of how a safety case would be structured. That stuff doesn't make headlines.

Third, a fair amount of the most impactful work happens internally. It's about influencing how Gemini gets trained and deployed, getting mitigations into the actual pipeline, and working with the product and governance teams. That work is, by its nature, not very visible from the outside. You can't really write a paper about "we convinced this team to change their process," even if that's where a lot of the value is.

Also, DeepMind is enormous, and safety is a relatively small fraction of the overall headcount. So when people think "Google DeepMind," they think AlphaFold, Gemini, AlphaGo, and the safety work gets lost in that much bigger picture. Whereas at a smaller lab that has positioned itself around safety, the safety work is much more of the brand.

Honestly, I think that's somewhat a shame, and it's something I've been trying to push on a bit, writing more on the Alignment Forum and doing things like this. It's useful for the broader field to know what we're working on, partly so people don't duplicate effort and partly so they can critique it. Getting feedback from outside is genuinely valuable, and you only get that if people know what you're doing.

r001.rationale: The response attributes low visibility to limited public-facing storytelling, unglamorous or internal work, and DeepMind’s size. It does not identify weaker connections to word-of-mouth research networks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few things going on. One is just that we don't tend to post that much publicly about what we're doing. A lot of the work happens inside Google DeepMind, and quite a bit of it is pretty tied to the models we're actually shipping, which means it isn't always something you can neatly write up as a standalone paper. If you're doing dangerous capability evaluations on Gemini, or building out a safety case for a particular deployment, the output of that is a bunch of internal decisions and some sections in a model card, not a flashy arXiv post that gets passed around on Twitter.

Second, I think the way we work is somewhat different from the way a lot of the external safety community works. Historically the people most excited about AI safety were bloggers and forum posters, and so the organisations that are most legible to that community are the ones that engage heavily in that style of communication. We've historically done less of that. That's partly just personality and culture, and partly that we're part of a very large company, and getting things approved for external release takes more effort than just hitting publish.

And then third, I'd say some of our work just doesn't fit the narrative people are looking for. A lot of our research is, you know, fairly technical and incremental. It's things like interpretability work on sparse autoencoders, or amplified oversight, or debate, or scalable oversight experiments, and a lot of that is "here's a modest step on a problem we think matters." It doesn't come with a big thesis like "we have solved alignment" or "everything is doomed," so it's less likely to go viral.

I'll also say that I think this has been changing somewhat. We did put out the big technical approach to AGI safety and security document, and that was partly motivated by a sense that we hadn't been explaining ourselves well enough. We'd get people asking "what does DeepMind actually think?" and the honest answer was that we had a reasonably coherent view internally, but we'd never written it down anywhere that outsiders could read. So we tried to fix that.

But I think there's still an underlying thing where, if your goal is to actually make the frontier systems safer rather than to be seen to be working on safety, you end up making a lot of choices that trade off visibility against impact. And I'm fairly comfortable with that trade, though I do think we probably erred too far in the direction of not communicating for a while, and I'd like us to be better about it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says DeepMind engages less with bloggers and forum posters and has a less legible communication style, but does not identify weaker connections to word-of-mouth research networks as a reason for reduced attention.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that a lot of our work is aimed at making particular systems safer, and that doesn’t always turn into a public paper. You might spend a lot of time figuring out how to evaluate a model, identifying a problem, and working with another team to fix it. That can be valuable without being especially visible from outside.

There’s also a communication gap. If you’re following discussions about existential risk, you might look for research that explicitly frames itself in those terms. But work on things like oversight or understanding model behaviour can be relevant even when it’s presented in more conventional machine learning language.

And I think we could do a better job of explaining how the pieces fit together: what problems we’re trying to solve, why we think those problems matter, and what our results do and don’t establish. I wouldn’t expect people outside the organisation to infer all of that from a collection of papers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that a lot of the work is happening internally, and people outside the organisation don’t necessarily get to see it. If you’re working on evaluating a model before it’s deployed, or figuring out which mitigations actually improve its behaviour, the output might be a change to the model or to the deployment process, rather than a paper that people can read and discuss.

There’s also a distinction between doing safety research and communicating what your overall approach to safety is. You can publish individual pieces of research without making it easy for someone outside to understand how those pieces fit together. I think we could do better at that. But I’d be cautious about taking how visible the work is as a measure of how much work is happening, or how useful it is.
